claims.text: Rapid solidification that refines eutectic lamellar spacing will simultaneously increase strength and ductility relative to conventional cooling.
Conventional casting with a standard cooling rate produces a relatively coarse lamellar architecture in the eutectic high-entropy alloy.
A controlled high cooling rate during solidification will refine the eutectic lamellar spacing.
The rapid-solidification and baseline samples should have the same alloy composition and environmental conditions.
The intervention should use a significantly higher, controlled cooling rate than the baseline.
Mechanical properties should be measured by standard tensile testing at room temperature.
Finer eutectic lamellae obstruct dislocation motion more effectively.
More effective obstruction of dislocation motion increases strength.
Finer eutectic lamellae distribute strain more uniformly between the soft and hard phases.
More uniform strain distribution maintains or enhances ductility.
Rapidly solidified samples will have higher yield strength than conventionally cooled samples.
Rapidly solidified samples will have total elongation equal to or greater than conventionally cooled samples.
The expected trend follows general microstructural-refinement principles.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant yield-strength increase together with equal or improved ductility would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis requires ductility to increase, whereas the predicted outcome and falsification rule allow ductility merely to remain equal to the baseline. Thus, unchanged ductility would satisfy the stated experimental criterion but not the original claim of simultaneously increased strength and ductility.
